Developing with AI coding agents

Source: vignettes/articles/ai-coding-agents.Rmd
ai-coding-agents.Rmd

This article is for developers who work on rdborrow with an AI coding agent such as Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, or Gemini CLI. The repository tells agents how the package is built, so the agent’s first draft follows the package’s conventions. Your job shifts to stating the task precisely and checking the result.

How agents learn the package’s conventions

AGENTS.md, at the top of the repository, is a plain markdown file of instructions that most coding agents read automatically. Claude Code reads .claude/CLAUDE.md instead, which imports AGENTS.md, so every agent follows the same rules from a single file. AGENTS.md is listed in .Rbuildignore, so it never ships with the package.

It covers:

Section What the agent learns
Architecture The user-facing API, the method class hierarchy, how estimate() dispatch works, and the _core() / _se() / _boot_statistic() pattern
Key commands How to run tests, re-document, build the site, and run R CMD check
Coding Base R only, base pipe, R 4.1 compatibility, checkmate validation, comment style
Testing Where tests go, which expectations to use, and that a bug fix needs a failing test first
Documentation and NEWS.md When to add roxygen docs, pkgdown entries, and NEWS bullets
Specialized tasks Where to find the tidyverse instructions for argument checking and deprecation
Before committing The one-line validation command to run before every commit

For Claude Code, .claude/settings.json also pre-approves routine commands such as Rscript, grep, and gh issue view, so the agent doesn’t stop to ask before running tests.

A workflow that works

  1. Start from an issue. An issue gives the agent a fixed statement of the problem and gives the PR something to close.
  2. Ask for a plan before code. Reading a plan takes a minute; unwinding a wrong approach takes much longer.
  3. Write the test first. Have the agent write a test that fails for the right reason, and confirm it fails, before it touches the fix.
  4. Let the agent implement and validate. AGENTS.md tells it to run styler, re-document, and run the before-committing check.
  5. Review the diff yourself. Read every changed line, starting with the statistics.
  6. Open a PR that references the issue.

Example prompts

Add a method

Adding a new method is written so that an agent can follow it step by step. Give the agent the estimator’s definition and point it at the article:

Add a new primary-analysis estimator to rdborrow called ec_or(), an
outcome-regression estimator for external control borrowing as defined in
<paper, equation number>.

Follow vignettes/articles/adding-a-method.Rmd step by step and use
R/ec_ipw.R as the template. Before writing the estimator, write
tests/testthat/test-full_pipeline_ec_or.R against reference values that I
will provide, and confirm that it fails. Then implement the method until
the test passes and devtools::check() is clean.

Fix a bug from an issue 

Read issue #86 with `gh issue view 86 --comments`. Write a test that
reproduces the bug and confirm that it fails. Then fix the bug, add a
NEWS.md bullet, and run the before-committing check.

Deprecate an argument 

Deprecate the <argument> argument of <function>(), following the
deprecation instructions referenced in AGENTS.md. Update the tests and
NEWS.md.

Checking the agent’s work

An agent can produce a clean, passing, well-documented change that is statistically wrong. These habits catch that:

  • Supply the reference values yourself. Take them from the paper, the authors’ code, or a hand calculation. An agent that writes both the estimator and its expected output can encode the same mistake in both.
  • Review the math line by line. For an estimator, that is .{name}_core() and .{name}_se(); the rest is plumbing.
  • Keep changes additive. A new estimator adds files and edits only the registration spots listed in Adding a new method. If the diff changes the logic of run_analysis(), an existing method, or a shared helper, ask why.
  • Treat a changed regression test as a red flag. The test-full_pipeline_*.R files lock every method’s output on SyntheticData. A changed number needs an explanation in the PR.
  • Run the full check. devtools::test() uses load_all(), which can hide problems that only appear in the installed package. devtools::check() doesn’t.

Testing the docs with an adversarial agent

Docs written for agents can be tested by an agent. To check this article, Adding a new method, and AGENTS.md, we gave a second agent a real task: build ec_or(), an outcome-regression estimator for the primary analysis with bootstrap-only inference, in its own git worktree. Its instructions said to use only the docs, to log every time it had to read package code instead, and to treat a run with no findings as suspicious.

The agent built a working method on its own branch:

  • An independent reference script, written in base R before any package code, and the new ec_or() agreed exactly on SyntheticData.
  • The full-pipeline test failed first and passed after implementation. devtools::check() reported 0 errors, 0 warnings, and 0 notes, and ec_or() ran inside run_simulation().
  • It reported 15 findings. Two were blockers, places where it couldn’t continue without reading code: the docs didn’t say that estimate() should rename columns to S and A with .build_analysis_df(), and they didn’t give .run_bootstrap()’s arguments or return value. Both are now documented, along with the missing registration spots and a bootstrap-only example.
  • It found two package bugs, both since fixed: bootstrap = 1 was accepted and then failed with an opaque error (#91), and run_simulation() silently recycled a vector true_effect across replicates (#90).

Rerun this check whenever the developer docs change. The prompt below is the one we used, updated with what the first run taught us:

You are an adversarial tester for the rdborrow R package's developer
documentation. Build a new borrowing method by following the docs exactly,
and report every place they are wrong, ambiguous, or missing something. A
smooth run with no findings is a suspicious result; look harder.

Setup:
- Create a git worktree on a new branch from the branch under test. Do not
  touch any other branch or the main working tree. Building from a
  worktree adds a `.git` file at the top level; add `^\.git$` to your
  branch's .Rbuildignore and note that this edit is a test artifact.
- Your only guidance is AGENTS.md, vignettes/articles/adding-a-method.Rmd,
  and vignettes/articles/ai-coding-agents.Rmd. You may read package code,
  but every time you need code to learn something the docs should have
  told you, log it as a finding.
- Do not push, open PRs, or create issues. There is no issue for this
  exercise; say so in the NEWS bullet instead of citing one.

Task: add <estimator>, defined as <definition>, with <sandwich or
bootstrap-only> inference. Choose a method that exercises a path the docs'
toy example does not.

Rules:
1. Before any package code, write an independent reference script in base
   R, with no rdborrow internals, that computes the estimate on
   SyntheticData. This is your ground truth.
2. Follow adding-a-method.Rmd in order. Write the full-pipeline test
   against the reference values first and confirm it fails.
3. Follow every AGENTS.md rule and run the "Before committing" one-liner.
   Commit locally.
4. Probe the docs' claims:
   - List every existing file you modified. Each one is either a step in
     the checklist or a finding.
   - Run the method inside run_simulation() with a few small simulated
     replicates and a scalar true_effect, and confirm which CI columns
     coverage uses.
   - Try to break the constructor (out-of-range arguments, bootstrap = 1,
     mismatched formula counts) and judge whether the errors are clear.

Report, most severe first: each finding with the doc file and line, what
it says, what happened, a suggested fix, and a severity (blocker, wrong,
gap, nit); files touched, split into checklist steps and undocumented
edits; reference vs. package estimates; the final devtools::check()
summary; and how long a human contributor would need with these docs.

Keeping AGENTS.md current

AGENTS.md is the single source of the package’s conventions for both people and agents. When a convention changes, update AGENTS.md in the same PR. Add new rules there, not to .claude/CLAUDE.md, so that every agent sees them.
